title: Politeness as a layer: ます and です

grammarPoints.rule: Polite verbs are built from the i-STEM: drop the final -u to the い row, then add ます. のむ → のみ + ます. る-verbs just drop る: たべる → たべ + ます. する → します, くる → きます. The MEANING doesn't change — たべる and たべます both mean 'eat'. Only the audience changes.

antiPattern.why: the る is dropped before ます — たべます, not たべるます

grammarPoints.rule: The polite negative swaps ます for ません — same stem, different tail. のみます → のみません. It is the polite twin of plain ない: のまない = のみません.

examples.ja: きょうは いきません

antiPattern.why: ません REPLACES ます — you don't stack ない on top of it

grammarPoints.rule: です finishes NOUNS politely, the way だ finishes them plainly: ねこだ → ねこです. です is NOT 'polite だ' you can bolt onto verbs — たべるです is not a sentence. Verbs get ます; nouns get です.

examples.ja: たなかさんは せんせいです

antiPattern.why: verbs take ます, not です — たべます

grammarPoints.rule: か turns a sentence into a question. In POLITE speech か is required — たべますか？ Plain speech usually drops it and just rises in pitch: たべる？ か after a plain sentence sounds blunt or archaic.

examples.ja: みずを のみますか
たなかさんは せんせいですか

antiPattern.why: the stem comes before ます — たべますか

grammarPoints.rule: Japanese picks its form by WHO you're talking to, not by what you mean. Friends and family get plain (たべる). Teachers, strangers, and customers get polite (たべます). Same thought, two skins — you choose by audience, every sentence.
